questions.stemHtml: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 2-week history of progressively severe pain in his right leg just below the knee. An x-ray of the involved area shows a large, partly calcified mass that erodes the medullary canal of the tibia, infiltrates the cortex, and extends into the adjacent soft tissue. A biopsy of the lesion identifies primitive cells in a lace-like meshwork of bone with numerous mitoses. Which of the following is another common site of origin for this pathologic process?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Osteosarcoma, the most common type of primary bone cancer, occurs most often in the second and third decades of life. It typically occurs in long bones, frequently above the knee in the distal femur or below the knee in the proximal tibia. The metaphysis is often affected. The initial presentation often includes pain and swelling; sometimes, a fragility fracture is the declaring presentation. Causes include familial malignancy syndromes (especially involving the retinoblastoma or P53 tumor suppressor genes), exposure to radiation, or bony dysplasia, such as fibrous dysplasia or osteitis deformans (Paget disease) in older adults. This malignancy is locally destructive to bone and can erode through the cortex resulting in a sunburst periosteal reaction and elevation of the periosteum (eg, Codman triangle) on plain x-rays. Once osteosarcoma is suspected, an MRI is indicated to evaluate the extent of local invasion and to allow for local staging. It arises from osteoblast-like mesenchymal cells that produce osteoid, the collagen matrix necessary for mineralization and bone formation. Thus, biopsy will show primitive cells with enlarged nuclei in a bed of disorganized tissue with areas of osteoid production. Osteosarcoma is an aggressive tumor with a poor prognosis. Treatment requires aggressive surgical resection as well as chemotherapy.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

The clavicle (Choice A) is not a common site of origin for bony neoplasms. Rare cases of giant cell tumors of the clavicle have been reported. These tumors present with a soap bubble appearance on x-rays and multinucleated giant cells on histology.

The metacarpal bones (Choice C) are a less common site of origin for bony neoplasms. Usually benign, the most common type is an enchondroma, which can also occur in the phalanges of the fingers. They are often painless and can be managed with observation alone. Ollier disease consists of multiple enchondromas that may present in a single extremity. Maffucci syndrome presents with multiple enchondromas and soft tissue angiomas.

The ribs (Choice D) are a less common site of origin for primary bony neoplasms. Metastatic lesions and myeloma are far more frequent. When primary lesions of the ribs arise, Ewing sarcoma and chondrosarcoma are the most commonly reported types. On histology, Ewing sarcoma shows multiple small, round, blue cells. X-rays may show elevated periosteum and layered neocortex formation (“onion skin” appearance). Chondrosarcoma histology will show lobules of hyaline-like cartilage and nests of malignant chondrocyte-like cells.

The vertebrae (Choice E) are common sites of metastases of breast and prostate cancer. Patients commonly present with pain that is worse at night and sclerotic lesions on x-rays. Multiple myeloma can also present in the vertebrae, often as multiple lytic lesions along with hypercalcemia, anemia, kidney failure, frequent infections, and diffuse skeletal pain. The most common primary bone tumor of the vertebrae is the osteoblastoma, a benign lesion that presents with bone pain that does not respond to aspirin.

Educational Objective: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary osseous malignancy in children, typically occurring in long bones, such as the distal femur and proximal tibia. Clinical findings include pain and swelling, with destruction of both medullary and cortical bone, a sunburst periosteal reaction, and elevation of the periosteum on radiography. Biopsy shows primitive, osteoblast-like cells in a network of osteoid. Treatment generally involves a combined surgical and medical approach.

questions.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of numbness in his hands and feet for 3 months. Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency is suspected. An increased serum concentration of which of the following is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: F.

Vitamin B12, or cobalamin, is a water-soluble B vitamin that is essential for DNA synthesis as well as the health of neural and hematopoietic tissue. Vitamin B12 acts as a cofactor for the conversion of homocysteine to methionine and the conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. Dietary sources of vitamin B12 primarily include animal sources such as meat, milk, or eggs.

Vitamin B12 deficiency is rarely caused by dietary deficiency, except in cases of strict veganism, and is more commonly encountered as a result of gastrointestinal malabsorption due to causes such as pernicious anemia, malabsorption following bariatric surgery, celiac or Crohn disease, bacterial small bowel overgrowth, or infection with the fish tapeworm Diphyllobothrium latum. Vitamin B12 deficiency presents with increased homocysteine, macrocytic anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils, and associated symptoms of generalized fatigue, pallor, and lightheadedness. Vitamin B12 deficiency can be distinguished from vitamin B9, or folic acid, deficiency by increased methylmalonate concentrations (normal in vitamin B9 deficiency) and the presence of neuropsychiatric symptoms, specifically subacute combined degeneration (SCD).

SCD is caused by demyelination of the dorsal columns, lateral corticospinal tracts, and spinocerebellar tracts, and presents with ataxic gait, muscle weakness, paresthesia, abnormal deep tendon reflexes, and loss of proprioception and vibration sense. Treatment is with vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) supplementation; however, if deficiency is prolonged, neural damage may be irreversible.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, and E.

Acetoacetate (Choice A), along with acetone and β-hydroxybutyrate, is produced by ketogenesis. Concentrations will be increased, therefore, during periods of fasting. Prolonged starvation is associated with fat and muscle wasting but not neurodegeneration.

Alanine (Choice B) and lactate (Choice C) concentrations are increased in pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency (PDCD); pyruvate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, facilitating transition into the citric acid cycle. PDCD is a rare inborn error of metabolism that presents with lactic acidosis, neurodevelopmental abnormalities and delay, hyperammonemia, tachypnea and hyperventilation, and hypotonia. Lactate (Choice C) is generated by anaerobic cell metabolism and thus increased concentrations are seen in a wide variety of conditions, including strenuous exercise, hypoxemia, shock, and mitochondrial dysfunction.

Leucine (Choice D) concentrations are increased in branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase deficiency, also termed maple syrup urine disease, which is characterized by abnormal degradation and consequent buildup of the branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine, and valine. It presents with severe neurologic defects, intellectual disability, vomiting, poor feeding, and a characteristic urine odor similar to maple syrup.

Methionine (Choice E) is generated by methionine synthase in a reaction that requires vitamin B12 as a coenzyme. Concentrations will be decreased, not increased, in vitamin B12 deficiency. Methionine concentrations are increased in cystathionine synthase deficiency, a form of homocystinuria, characterized by increased urine homocysteine, marfanoid habitus, osteoporosis, lens subluxation, atherosclerosis, and intellectual disability.

Causes include strict veganism and gastric malabsorption due to pernicious anemia, bariatric surgery, Crohn disease, or tapeworm infection. SCD results from demyelination of the dorsal columns, lateral corticospinal tracts, and spinocerebellar tracts, and presents with ataxic gait, muscle weakness, paresthesia, abnormal deep tendon reflexes, and loss of proprioception and vibration sense.

questions.stemHtml: A 20-year-old woman (III-1) comes to the physician for cancer risk assessment. She has a family history of breast cancer in her maternal grandfather and maternal aunt. Previous genetic analysis of the aunt showed a mutation in the BRCA2 gene. The patient's 45-year-old mother does not wish to undergo genetic testing. A pedigree is shown. Which of the following best represents the probability that this patient inherited the gene mutation in this family?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Most breast cancers are sporadic, but a minority are caused by germline mutations in BRCA1 or BRCA2, which are tumor suppressor genes. questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman comes to the physician for advice on a weight loss plan. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 86 kg (190 lb); BMI is 33 kg/m2. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. She has read an article on the Internet that outlines a balanced diet of 1500 kcal/day. She says, "It's not as strict of a diet as some of my friends have tried. I think I can follow it for a long time." At her current level of physical activity, she expends approximately 2500 kcal/day. Based on this information, this patient will most likely lose weight at which of the following rates?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C.

Balancing caloric intake versus caloric expenditure underlies many theories of weight loss, which are central to the treatment of obesity. In general, the recommended adult caloric intake is 2500 calories daily for men and 2000 calories daily for women, though these recommendations vary based on lifestyle, comorbidities, and caloric demand. One pound of body fat contains approximately 3500 calories. A daily caloric deficit of 1000 calories will therefore result in loss of 7000 calories during a 7-day period, resulting in a loss of 2 pounds of fat weekly. Weight loss has a variety of beneficial health effects in the setting of obesity, including reduced incidence of diabetes mellitus, depression, hypertension, and osteoarthritis.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

Choices A, B, D, and E represent erroneous calculations based on an incorrect assessment of the number of calories stored in 1 pound of body fat.

questions.stemHtml: A 56-year-old woman comes to the physician because of shortness of breath over the past several months. She smokes 2 packs of cigarettes daily and is not interested in quitting. Respirations are 24/min. She is barrel-chested. Breath sounds are decreased over all lung fields, and pulmonary function testing shows an obstructive pattern. Oxygen saturation on room air is 91% at rest and 82% with exercise. After telling the patient that her lungs show signs of damage from tobacco, which of the following approaches by the physician is most appropriate in beginning to address advance directives with this patient?

options.label: A
options.html: A.     "As long as you continue to smoke, it would be futile for me to be aggressive with your medical care."

options.label: B
options.html: B.     "Have you ever considered what medical treatment you would want if your breathing worsens?"

options.label: C
options.html: C.    "If you continue to smoke, you'll need to find a new physician."

options.label: D
options.html: D.     "In my experience, people with your type of lung damage do not do well when put on mechanical ventilation. I'm sure you wouldn't want a tube in your throat, would you?"

options.label: E
options.html: E.     "It is very important that I make plans for your future health care."

options.label: F
options.html: F.     "You are shortening your life span. We need to discuss what medical treatment you want."

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Advance directives are formal specifications of a patient’s wishes, created and executed during a time of decision-making capacity. Advance directives should reflect a patient’s wishes as expressed during periods of stable values and preferences. They are enacted when the patient loses capacity to communicate preferences about healthcare wishes. Often, these documents govern end-of-life care and are commonly used in cases of terminal illness; late-stage chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is a very common time of use. The physician should ask open-ended questions to assess the patient’s wishes and values. Open-ended questioning honors the patient’s autonomy. The medicolegal strength of an advance directive is greater when family members or persons who know the patient corroborate the document’s accurate reflection of long-standing and stable wishes.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, E, and F.

Ending medical treatment (Choice A) or terminating care with this patient (Choice C) are paternalistic approaches that constitute abandonment. Giving patients ultimatums or conditions for receiving care opposes the ethical principle of altruism. Physicians must honor patients’ autonomy in end-of-life medical decisions.

Though the physician may give the patient information about mechanical ventilation outcomes later in the conversation (Choice D), the physician should first ask the patient about her care preferences in an open-ended way. The question is not open-ended or autonomy-promoting in that the physician is expressing their own opinion about the best option for the patient.

Stating that the physician needs to make plans for the patient’s care (Choice E) constitutes a paternalistic approach that disinvites the patient’s collaboration. The physician should ask open-ended questions to honor the patient’s autonomy and assess her values.

Stating that the patient is shortening her life span (Choice F) is a judgmental statement that may make the patient feel bad about herself and preclude open discussion about her end-of-life care preferences. Open discussion is important for promoting patient autonomy.

Educational Objective: All discussions about advance directives or other end-of-life care should begin with the physician asking open-ended, non-leading, non-judgmental questions to explore the patient’s end-of-life preferences and values. This approach honors the patient’s autonomy.

questions.stemHtml: A 48-year-old woman comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. Her husband of 20 years died 2 years ago. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. During the examination, the patient mentions that she has begun dating again. It is most appropriate for the physician to counsel this patient about which of the following?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Physicians should counsel sexually active patients about safe sex practices to decrease the risk for sexually transmitted infection. Safe sex practices include limiting the number of sexual partners, receiving human papillomavirus vaccinations, being aware of and disclosing sexually transmitted infection status, and utilizing barrier protection such as condoms or diaphragms. For female patients of reproductive age who are dating male partners, discussing a safe sex method that concurrently decreases the risk for unwanted pregnancy is appropriate. Condoms both decrease sexually transmitted infection and pregnancy risk. Safe sex practices should be discussed with patients regardless of gender identity and sexual preference, in non-judgmental terms focused on keeping the patient and partner healthy.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Cohabitation (Choice A) refers to partners living together. Though the physician may explore the patient’s preferences regarding this personal decision, counseling the patient about cohabitation is generally outside of the physician’s scope of practice.

Couples counseling (Choice C) is appropriate for committed couples experiencing interpersonal difficulties. This patient has not mentioned interpersonal conflict or a committed relationship.

An increased frequency of sexual intercourse (Choice D) does confer an increased risk for sexually transmitted infection and pregnancy. However, without a condom, even infrequent sexual intercourse can lead to sexually transmitted infection or pregnancy. Further, condom use can mitigate these risks while enabling this patient to pursue sexual intercourse as she desires.

Oral contraceptive use (Choice E) prevents unwanted pregnancy. However, oral contraceptive pills do not protect against sexually transmitted infections.

Educational Objective: Physicians should counsel sexually active patients about safe sex practices, including utilizing barrier protection such as condoms. Condoms both decrease sexually transmitted infection and pregnancy risk.

questions.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of dry mouth, muscle weakness, constipation, inability to achieve an erection, and progressive fatigue. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years. His temperature is 36.7°C (98°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 10/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Neurologic examination shows weakness of the deltoids, biceps, iliopsoas, and quadriceps, and absence of all muscle stretch reflexes. Sensation to all modalities is normal. A chest x-ray shows a right lung mass. Laboratory studies show antibodies directed against the P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel. Which of the following mechanisms is the most likely cause of the neurologic findings in this patient?

options.label: A
options.html: A.      Blockade of motor nerve conduction

options.label: B
options.html: B.    Central inhibition of α-motoneuron firing

options.label: D
options.html: D.      Hyperpolarization of the muscle membrane

options.label: E
options.html: E.     Impaired acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

Impaired acetylcholine (ACh) release at the neuromuscular junction is associated with myasthenic (Lambert-Eaton) syndrome. Myasthenic syndrome is an autoimmune condition in which autoantibodies directed against voltage-gated calcium channels in the presynaptic neuron decrease the release of ACh. Limited ACh release limits muscle cell depolarization and results in proximal muscle weakness. Additional symptoms include hyporeflexia, constipation, and autonomic dysregulation. With extended use, muscle strength improves as a result of the gradual accumulation of ACh in the synapse with repeated presynaptic depolarization. Diagnosis can be confirmed with testing for anti-voltage-gated calcium channel antibodies or electromyography testing. In many cases, myasthenic syndrome is a paraneoplastic syndrome associated with small cell lung carcinoma.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Blockade of motor nerve conduction (Choice A) is associated with the development of ACh receptors antibodies in myasthenia gravis. In myasthenia gravis, these antibodies target postsynaptic ACh receptors, preventing ACh binding, and inhibiting nerve conduction. Patients present with ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia, and muscle weakness, which are worse with repetitive activity and later in the day. Neostigmine is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, which decreases the breakdown of ACh in the neuromuscular synaptic junction and increases its duration of action used in the treatment of myasthenia gravis.

Central inhibition of α-motoneuron firing (Choice B) is associated with antagonist muscle groups in spinal reflexes. Spinal reflexes are associated with afferent neurons that synapse with Renshaw cells, specialized inhibitory interneurons, which prevent antagonist muscle firing by α-motoneuron. This is not associated with the development of myasthenic syndrome.

Decreased excitation-contraction coupling (Choice C) at the neuromuscular endplate would prevent release of calcium from voltage-gated ion channels and prevent or limit muscular contraction. Decreased excitation-contraction coupling is the not the primary cause of myasthenic syndrome.

Hyperpolarization of the muscle membrane (Choice D) is associated with sodium-potassium channels in cardiac myocytes that use energy to transfer sodium out of the cell and potassium into the cell, creating a negative resting potential. During depolarization, sodium flows into cardiac myocytes, which triggers a contraction in a coordinated fashion.

Educational Objective: Myasthenic (Lambert-Eaton) syndrome is caused by antibodies directed against voltage-gated calcium channels, which decrease the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction. This leads to decreased reflexes, muscle weakness that improves with repeated use, and autonomic instability. It is frequently a paraneoplastic syndrome associated with small cell lung cancer.

questions.stemHtml: A 2-month-old male newborn is brought to the emergency department because of noisy and difficult breathing for 6 hours. Laryngoscopy shows multiple, slender, finger-like excrescences on both vocal cords. The newborn's condition is most likely caused by maternal infection with which of the following during pregnancy?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a common human pathogen that infects epithelial cells and can cause a variety of lesions. Infection with low-risk strains (subtypes 6 and 11) can cause warty neoplasms (soft, fleshy papules), and infection with high-risk strains (subtypes 16, 18, 31, and 33) can cause dysplastic and malignant lesions. HPV is primarily transmitted through direct contact. In children, the most common vector for HPV infection is transmission from an affected mother during labor and transit through the birth canal with consequent infection of the larynx or oropharynx, though the presence of these lesions may also raise concern for sexual assault in the correct clinical context. Laryngeal papillomatosis frequently affects the vocal cords and presents as a vocal cord nodule or growths. Presentations include dysphonia (hoarseness) and may progress to stridor, dyspnea, chronic cough, dysphagia, globus sensation, and airway obstruction if the lesion becomes large enough. Risk factors for clinically significant HPV infection include immunodeficiency and injury to the epithelium from another cause (eg, trauma, coinfection). Treatment focuses on maintaining a patent airway, surgical removal of symptomatic lesions, and preserving voice quality. Anogenital manifestations of HPV infection are common and include condyloma acuminata and dysplasia or carcinoma of the vulva, cervix, penis, or anus. Non-anogenital manifestations include verruca vulgaris and plantar warts.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Chlamydia trachomatis (Choice A) is a common causative agent of neonatal bacterial conjunctivitis, along with N. gonorrhoeae. Chlamydial conjunctivitis presents within 5 to 14 days of birth and is characterized by watery eye discharge. All newborns should receive topical antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent conjunctivitis; erythromycin, which binds the bacterial 50s ribosomal subunit and prevents bacterial protein synthesis, is commonly used.

Herpes simplex virus (Choice B) (HSV) infection is characterized by tender vesicles followed by ulceration and crusting. Manifestations of fetal infections include localized cutaneous lesions of the skin, eyes, and mouth, as well as systemic presentations such as meningoencephalitis. Transmission can occur via the placenta or through direct inoculation as the newborn passes through the birth canal in a mother with active lesions. Though the presence of HSV can result in more aggressive laryngeal papillomatosis, the causative agent is HPV.

HIV (Choice C) presents nonspecifically with fever, lymphadenopathy, gastrointestinal upset, and occasionally, rash. Neonatal infection results in an immunocompromised state that puts the newborn at risk for failure to thrive, recurrent infections, and chronic diarrhea. HIV does not directly cause laryngeal papillomatosis; rather, an impaired immune system can result in more severe HPV lesions.

Treponema pallidum (Choice E) can cause congenital syphilis via transmission through the placenta in the second and third trimesters. Manifestations include syphilitic rhinitis (eg, mucopurulent nasal discharge), rhagades, dental malformations (notched teeth and irregularly shaped molars), and hepatomegaly with or without splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy. The time of presentation after birth is variable.

Educational Objective: Vocal cord cutaneous neoplasms in the neonatal period are most likely caused by human papillomavirus, which infects epithelial cells and is responsible for a variety of mucocutaneous lesions, ranging from benign to malignant. Presentations include dysphonia (hoarseness) and may progress to stridor, dyspnea, chronic cough, dysphagia, globus sensation, and airway obstruction if the lesion becomes large enough. Treatment focuses on maintaining a patent airway, surgical removal of symptomatic lesions, and preserving voice quality.

All newborns should receive topical antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent conjunctivitis; erythromycin, which binds the bacterial 50s ribosomal subunit and prevents bacterial protein synthesis, is commonly used.

Herpes simplex virus (Choice B) (HSV) infection is characterized by tender vesicles followed by ulceration and crusting. Manifestations of fetal infections include localized cutaneous lesions of the skin, eyes, and mouth, as well as systemic presentations such as meningoencephalitis. Transmission can occur via the placenta or through direct inoculation as the newborn passes through the birth canal in a mother with active lesions. Though the presence of HSV can result in more aggressive laryngeal papillomatosis, the causative agent is HPV.

HIV (Choice C) presents nonspecifically with fever, lymphadenopathy, gastrointestinal upset, and occasionally, rash. Neonatal infection results in an immunocompromised state that puts the newborn at risk for failure to thrive, recurrent infections, and chronic diarrhea. HIV does not directly cause laryngeal papillomatosis; rather, an impaired immune system can result in more severe HPV lesions.

Treponema pallidum (Choice E) can cause congenital syphilis via transmission through the placenta in the second and third trimesters. Manifestations include syphilitic rhinitis (eg, mucopurulent nasal discharge), rhagades, dental malformations (notched teeth and irregularly shaped molars), and hepatomegaly with or without splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy. The time of presentation after birth is variable.

Presentations include dysphonia (hoarseness) and may progress to stridor, dyspnea, chronic cough, dysphagia, globus sensation, and airway obstruction if the lesion becomes large enough. Treatment focuses on maintaining a patent airway, surgical removal of symptomatic lesions, and preserving voice quality.

questions.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after he fell off a ladder from a height of 10 feet. His pulse is 70/min, and blood pressure is 125/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows multiple ecchymoses over the upper extremities and trunk. In response to the injury, activation of the endothelium of this patient's blood vessels has most likely resulted in which of the following?

options.label: D
options.html: D.        Decreased tissue plasminogen activator concentration

options.label: F
options.html: F.      Increased von Willebrand factor concentration

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: F.

Primary hemostasis is the process by which a platelet plug is formed following endothelial damage. Immediately following an injury, the damaged endothelial cells release endothelin, which leads to transient vasoconstriction and stimulates platelet aggregation at the site of injury, along with von Willebrand factor (VWF), which is also released from the alpha granules of platelets. VWF binds to exposed collagen on the damaged endothelium and tethers the platelets to the endothelium via interaction with the Gp1b receptor on the platelet surface, promoting primary hemostasis. In deficiency, von Willebrand disease arises. Von Willebrand disease is one of the most common hereditary bleeding disorders and caused by quantitative or qualitative abnormality of VWF, leading to impaired primary hemostasis. This can present with epistaxis, gingival bleeding, petechiae, easy bruising, and menorrhagia. Laboratory studies will show a normal platelet count and a prolonged bleeding time. Treatment depends on the site and severity of bleeding and may include desmopressin (which promotes release of additional VWF from endothelial cells) or administration of VWF concentrates, especially in the setting of traumatic injury or active bleeding.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, and E.

Decreased ADP concentration (Choice A) is incorrect, as there would instead be an increased ADP concentration following endothelial injury. ADP acts as a stimulator of platelet aggregation and clot formation. Binding of ADP to platelet receptors induces conformational changes in platelets, leading to release of platelet granules. Additionally, ADP induces platelets to form thromboxane A2 via the action of cyclooxygenase and thromboxane A2 synthase. Decreased thromboxane A2 concentration (Choice C) is therefore incorrect. Thromboxane A2 is a potent stimulator of further platelet activation and recruitment.

Decreased GTP concentration (Choice B) is incorrect. Increase in GTP via conversion from GDP is necessary for activation of signaling pathways that play a crucial role in platelet activity.

Decreased tissue plasminogen activator concentration (Choice D) is incorrect. Hemostasis and restoration of perfusion is a balance between thrombosis and thrombolysis. Tissue plasminogen activator would be activated in the setting of thrombolysis because of the presence of a thrombus; however, this principle is not the key related to endothelial injury in primary hemostasis.

Increased cGMP concentration (Choice E) would lead to inhibition of platelet function, thus preventing the formation of the platelet plug. This would cause ongoing bleeding and is incorrect.

Educational Objective: Increased von Willebrand factor (VWF) concentration is seen after endothelial damage and plays an important role in primary hemostasis by linking platelets to the damaged endothelium. Deficiency of VWF leads to impaired primary hemostasis and can manifest as easy bruising and increased mucosal bleeding.

questions.stemHtml: During a study of primary human hepatocytes, it is found that these cells dedifferentiate when grown in culture and lose many of the synthetic and metabolic functions unique to in vivo hepatocytes. Coculturing the primary hepatocytes with biliary epithelial cells preserves many aspects of the differentiated state of the hepatocytes. Compared with hepatocytes grown alone, the cocultured hepatocytes most likely produce an increased amount of which of the following?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

Hepatocytes are involved many metabolic processes, including metabolism of nitrogenous waste via the urea cycle. The urea cycle allows for the conversion of toxic nitrogenous waste products, such as ammonia, into urea, which can be safely excreted by the kidneys.

Failure of the urea cycle leads to an accumulation of ammonia which contributes to hepatic encephalopathy. In the described experiment, preservation of hepatocyte differentiation via co-culturing with biliary cells will maintain normal hepatocyte metabolic processes, including production of urea. In contrast, dedifferentiated hepatocytes will maintain core metabolic pathways that are common to most cells, such as glycolysis and mitochondrial respiration, but will lose the metabolic functions that are specific to hepatocytes, such as the urea cycle, amino acid deamination and transamination, gluconeogenesis, and synthesis of albumin and coagulation factors.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Alanine (Choice A) is a non-essential amino acid that is produced by transamination of pyruvate. It plays a key role in the glucose-alanine cycle, which allows muscle fibers to convert amino groups to glutamate and then to alanine, which is metabolized by the liver for gluconeogenesis. Co-cultured hepatocytes would be expected to consume a greater amount of alanine, rather than produce it.

Fructose (Choice B) is a monosaccharide. It is absorbed into hepatocytes by the GLUT-2 transporter. In contrast to glucose, which is utilized throughout the body, the metabolism of fructose by fructolysis takes place specifically in the liver. Differentiated hepatocytes would be expected to metabolize a greater amount of fructose, rather than producing it.

Maltose (Choice C) is a disaccharide formed from two units of glucose. Maltose is cleaved by maltase into two units of glucose in the intestinal brush border and is not directly metabolized by the liver. Neither differentiated nor de-differentiated human cells produce maltose, although both may utilize glucose for energy.

Pyruvate (Choice D), the conjugate base of pyruvic acid, is a central compound in human metabolism that serves as an intermediary between glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, gluconeogenesis, lactate metabolism, and glucose-alanine pathways. Its production through glycolysis would not differ between dedifferentiated and differentiated hepatocytes.

The urea cycle allows for the conversion of toxic nitrogenous waste products into urea, which can be safely excreted by the kidneys. Loss of hepatocyte differentiation could lead to the loss of metabolic functions that are specific to hepatocytes, such as the urea cycle, amino acid deamination and transamination, gluconeogenesis, and synthesis of albumin and coagulation factors.

questions.stemHtml: A male newborn has multiple dysmorphic features suggestive of Down syndrome. Chromosomal analysis is ordered. Which of the following choices is most appropriate regarding what the parents should be told?

options.label: A
options.html: A.    The newborn has some features of Down syndrome, and chromosomal analysis has been requested

options.label: B
options.html: B.       The newborn has some unusual features on examination, and a test has been ordered that may help determine a diagnosis

options.label: C
options.html: C.      The physician's concerns should not be mentioned because the parents would worry unnecessarily if the physician is wrong

options.label: D
options.html: D.      Some tests have been ordered, the results of which will be communicated at the routine 2-week examination of the newborn

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A.

Physicians should address objective findings by explaining their differential diagnosis and the next diagnostic steps in simple language that is delivered in small pieces. It is important that physicians honor patients’ and family members’ autonomy by providing them with relevant clinical information. Typically, the most relevant information includes the most likely diagnoses and the most serious diagnoses. As Down Syndrome is both likely and serious, the physician should discuss this possibility and provide timely updates about diagnostic results.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, and D.

Providing vague or misleading information about the differential diagnosis and diagnostic process, (Choices B and D) or withholding information (Choice C) are paternalistic approaches that avoid giving the patient’s family relevant clinical information. Physicians may be tempted to protect patients and family members from hearing distressing news; however, delivering bad news early and allowing the patient and family to process the information with the physician is the most therapeutic approach. Additionally, stating the tests will be discussed at a “routine” visit is dishonest in implying that the newborn’s development is normal.

Educational Objective: Physicians should address objective findings by explaining their differential diagnosis and the next diagnostic steps in simple language that is delivered in small pieces. Physicians should aim to provide patients and family members with relevant clinical information.

questions.stemHtml: A healthy 58-year-old man comes to the physician because of progressive hair loss during the past few years. He says that his father and grandfathers had a similar pattern of baldness. Examination of the scalp shows hair loss in an "M-" shaped pattern over the frontal hairline. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the hair loss in this patient?

options.label: B
options.html: B.       Dihydrotestosterone binding to androgen receptors

options.label: C
options.html: C.      Increased activity of cytochrome P450 aromatase

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Dihydrotestosterone binding to androgen receptors is the primary mechanism of male pattern baldness, or androgenic alopecia. Testosterone is converted to dihydrotestosterone, a more potent androgen, by 5α-reductase. When androgen receptors in terminal hair follicles are exposed to dihydrotestosterone, hair follicles undergo miniaturization and may transition to fine vellus hairs causing the clinical presentation of androgenic alopecia. Androgenic alopecia is progressive, and most prominent in the frontal and vertex scalp locations. Finasteride, which is a 5α-reductase inhibitor, is used in the treatment of androgenic alopecia.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, and D.

Decreased 5α-reductase activity (Choice A) prevents conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone and does not cause androgenic alopecia. Androgenic alopecia is driven by the presence of dihydrotestosterone.

Increased activity of cytochrome P450 aromatase (Choice C) promotes peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogens. Increased availability of estrogens does not worsen androgenic alopecia.  Increased availability of estrogens may instead result in the development of biologic female secondary sex characteristics, such as gynecomastia.

Increased testicular testosterone production (Choice D) increases the amount of testosterone available for conversion to dihydrotestosterone; however, this is not the primary mechanism of androgenic alopecia.

Educational Objective: Androgenetic alopecia is caused by dihydrotestosterone binding to androgen receptors in terminal hair follicles. Over time, dihydrotestosterone promotes terminal hair follicle miniaturization and transition to vellus hairs. Androgenic alopecia progresses over several years and commonly involves the frontal and vertex scalp.

questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man volunteers as a subject for a cardiac function study. Vital signs and a physical examination are obtained. Echocardiography shows thickening of muscle tissue of the left ventricle. Subsequent testing is most likely to show which of the following underlying conditions in this man?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C.

Hypertension is a common cause of chronic systolic and diastolic dysfunction, and chronic hypertension is associated with left ventricular hypertrophy as a result of constant work against an increased afterload. The thickened myocardium results in impaired left ventricular relaxation and increased diastolic filling pressures that lead to left atrial enlargement and heart failure over time. Physical examination may show an S4 gallop suggestive of a stiff and noncompliant left ventricle. Jugular venous distension and pulmonary crackles indicate impaired forward flow of blood. An ECG may show evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy and left atrial enlargement. Adequate control of blood pressure decreases afterload and reduces the degree of cardiac myocyte hypertrophy, which decreases the risk for developing heart failure.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

Aortic regurgitation (Choice A) is commonly associated with endocarditis, acute rheumatic fever, and aortic root dilation. The ECG will show retrograde flow of blood into the left ventricle from the aortic root immediately after systole.

Coronary artery disease (Choice B) is a common comorbidity encountered in clinical practice that can lead to myocardial ischemia and infarction. The ECG may show regions of hypokinesis or akinesis that represent previously infarcted myocardium.

Mitral stenosis (Choice D), which presents with a murmur classically heard as an opening snap followed by a diastolic rumble, is associated with left atrial hypertrophy, and reduced left ventricular stroke volume due to decreased filling. These findings may be observed on the ECG.

Mitral valve prolapse (Choice E) is a cause of mitral regurgitation, typically presenting with a holosystolic murmur best heard in the left fourth or fifth intercostal space along the midclavicular line and radiates to the left axilla. The ECG may show abnormal positioning, movement, and/or thickening of the mitral valve leaflets.

Educational Objective: Hypertension is a common cause of chronic systolic and diastolic dysfunction, and chronic hypertension is associated with left ventricular hypertrophy as a result of constant work against an increased afterload.

questions.stemHtml: A 36-year-old man with sarcoidosis comes to the emergency department because of a 3-hour history of severe left flank pain radiating to his groin. He says the pain varies in intensity but never ceases completely. His temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 144/92 mm Hg. Physical examination shows left flank tenderness. Serum studies show a calcium concentration of 11.2 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows microscopic blood. Which of the following mechanisms is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?

options.label: C
options.html: C.     Increased intestinal absorption of oxalate

options.label: D
options.html: D.     Inhibition of urinary calcium excretion

options.label: E
options.html: E.     Stimulation of parathyroid hormone secretion

options.label: F
options.html: F.       Upregulation of vitamin D receptors

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Sarcoidosis is a noncaseating granulomatous disorder that may involve a variety of organ systems, in particular the lungs, and is prevalent in young adults of both sexes in Northern European, African, and African American populations. The clinical presentation ranges widely and depends on the affected organ system. Particularly frequent signs and symptoms include fatigue, uveitis, shortness of breath, cough, hepatosplenomegaly, arthritis, lymphadenopathy, and erythema nodosum. Hypercalcemia is a common feature of sarcoidosis. Sarcoid granulomas express increased activity of α1-hydroxylase, leading to increased concentrations of 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D with subsequent increased calcium absorption from the gastrointestinal lumen.

Hypercalcemia in sarcoidosis may lead to nephrolithiasis, as in this patient. Hypercalcemia may also manifest with abdominal discomfort and psychiatric disturbances. The treatment of nephrolithiasis varies depending on the size and location of the calculus, and complicating features. Small, uncomplicated calculi often pass without intervention, whereas large, obstructing, or infected calculi may require antibiotics, surgical removal, ureteral stenting, or percutaneous nephrostomy.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, E, and F.

Activation of osteoclast-activating factor (Choice A) is incorrect. Osteoclast-activating factor, better known as interleukin (IL)-1 beta, is an inflammatory cytokine that plays a role in induction of fever. While a variety of cytokines are involved in granulomatous inflammation, IL-1 beta is not prominent among them and does not play a commonly understood role in the pathophysiology of hypercalcemia in sarcoidosis.

Increased intestinal absorption of oxalate (Choice C) is incorrect. While oxalate is an important component of calcium oxalate renal calculi, the most likely cause of nephrolithiasis in patients with sarcoidosis is hypercalcemia, rather than an excess of oxalate.

Inhibition of urinary calcium excretion (Choice D) is incorrect. Patients with sarcoidosis do not typically display impaired urinary calcium excretion and frequently manifest both hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria.

Stimulation of parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion (Choice E) is incorrect. PTH is secreted in response to hypocalcemia detected by parathyroid gland calcium-sensing receptors. It then acts to increase serum calcium by increasing osteoclast activity, intestinal absorption, and renal tubular absorption. PTH concentrations in sarcoidosis are typically normal or decreased.

Upregulation of vitamin D receptors (Choice F) is incorrect. The hypercalcemia that may be observed in patients with sarcoidosis is caused by granulomatous expression of α1-hydroxylase, rather than overexpression of the vitamin D receptor.

Educational Objective: Sarcoidosis is a multisystemic disorder characterized by the presence of noncaseating granulomas. Hypercalcemia is common in sarcoidosis. Sarcoid granulomas express increased activity of α1-hydroxylase, leading to increased concentrations of 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D with subsequent increased calcium absorption from the gastrointestinal lumen. Hypercalcemia may lead to nephrolithiasis as well as abdominal pain and psychiatric disturbances.

questions.stemHtml: An investigator is studying a substance abuse problem among school-age children that involves taking large doses of over-the-counter cough medication containing dextromethorphan. The effects range from mild excitement with hallucinations to a sense of complete dissociation from the body. The investigator notes that this substance is an N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor antagonist. The psychological effects of this substance most closely resemble those of which of the following?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Both dextromethorphan and ketamine antagonize N-methyl-d
-aspartate (NMDA) glutamate receptors in the central nervous system (CNS). Dextromethorphan is a common ingredient in antitussive medications. When used in excess, it can have mild opioid-like effects and act as a dissociative hallucinogen. Dissociation is defined as a sense of detachment from one’s body and/or surroundings. Patients may experience altered consciousness and hallucinations. Similarly, ketamine causes dissociation. Ketamine has been historically used as an anesthetic and analgesic agent and has recently gained popularity as a rapid-acting antidepressant. Other NMDA antagonists include phencyclidine (another recreational drug associated with dissociation) and memantine (a neuroprotective agent that protects patients with dementia against glutamate excitotoxicity).

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Codeine (Choice A) is an opioid agonist used as an analgesic and antitussive. When used recreationally, codeine can lead to dissociative effects. However, codeine does not antagonize NMDA glutamate receptors, and ketamine more commonly leads to dissociation.

Methamphetamine (Choice C) is a CNS stimulant that causes release of dopamine, serotonin, and norepinephrine, leading to increased sympathetic tone (eg, tachycardia, hypertension, pupillary dilation, restlessness). Though methamphetamine-induced psychosis (eg, delusions, hallucinations) is possible, dissociation is less common. Methamphetamine is not considered a hallucinogen and is not a ligand of NMDA glutamate receptors.

Propofol (Choice D) is a sedative-hypnotic agent used in general anesthesia. It causes sedation by acting on CNS γ-aminobutyric acid receptors. Propofol is not associated with dissociation.

Tetrahydrocannabinol (Choice E) is a hallucinogen that acts on the endocannabinoid system in the CNS to cause euphoria, paranoia, hallucinations, increased appetite, conjunctival injection, and cognitive slowing. Dissociation is less common, and tetrahydrocannabinol is not a ligand of NMDA receptors.

questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old man has a history of cerebellar hemangioblastoma and retinal angiomas. Urinalysis shows microscopic blood. A CT scan of the abdomen shows a renal mass, and a nephrectomy is performed. The cut surface of the resected kidney is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is an adenocarcinoma of tubular epithelial cells. RCC is a common primary malignancy of the kidney and generally occurs in older, male smokers. It can present with gross or microscopic hematuria, flank pain, weight loss, or fever. Laboratory studies may show polycythemia or hypercalcemia as a result of associated paraneoplastic syndrome production of erythropoietin or parathyroid hormone-related peptide.

Hypercalcemia can also result from bony metastasis. Diagnosis of RCC typically occurs with CT scan or MRI and is confirmed by biopsy at the time of nephrectomy. Biopsy of RCC is characterized by the presence of polygonal clear cells as a result of the accumulation of lipid and carbohydrate in the cells. On gross pathology, there is typically a golden color caused by intracellular lipid accumulation. Adenocarcinoma is often well-circumscribed, centered on the renal cortex, and if large, may distort the kidney contour. There also may be hemorrhage, necrosis, calcification, or cystic change. It spreads hematogenously, and commonly presents as a metastatic neoplasm. The brain is a frequent site of metastasis.

In this example, this patient is less than 50 years of age and has had multiple tumors involving other body systems. This is suggestive of a genetic or hereditary cause of malignancy, in this case, likely von Hippel-Lindau syndrome.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Hemangioma (Choice A) refers to a benign proliferation of blood vessels, which can either be present at birth or develop shortly after birth. They are bright red in appearance and do not typically progress to malignancy.

Metastatic bronchogenic carcinoma (Choice B) is a malignant neoplasm of the lung. While a metastatic lesion from the lung cannot be excluded, the systemic nature of tumors in multiple systems and known association of renal cell carcinoma with von Hippel-Lindau disease makes a separate renal primary tumor more likely.

Myelolipomas (Choice C) are benign tumors that typically occur in the adrenal glands. They consist of adipose tissue and myeloid tissue. This patient’s tumor is in the kidney, not the adrenal gland, which lies above the kidney.

Transitional cell carcinoma (Choice E) is located within the urinary collecting system and bladder. The transitional epithelium of the collecting system and bladder is specialized stratified epithelium that can expand and contract depending on the collecting system volume. This patient’s lesion appears to arise from the renal cortical or medullary parenchyma, as opposed to the collecting system.

Educational Objective: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) often presents in older, male smokers, and the brain is a common site of metastasis. Biopsy of RCC is uniquely characterized by polygonal clear cells, caused by the accumulation of lipid and carbohydrate content in the cells. It is associated with cancer syndromes such as von Hippel-Lindau disease, which also presents with multiple vascular tumors.

questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after the sudden onset of tearing chest pain that radiates to his back. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. His pulse is 115/min, and blood pressure is 170/110 mm Hg. Physical examination and a chest radiograph show no abnormalities. Contrast axial (left) and sagittal (right) CT scans of the chest and abdomen shown confirm thoracoabdominal dissection of the aorta; the arrows indicate the vessel perfused by the false lumen. Occlusion of this vessel will most likely result in compromised blood flow to which of the following organs?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

This patient with tearing chest pain, hypertension, and CT scans showing  a dual lumen and flap within the arterial vasculature has an aortic dissection. Aortic dissections begin with a tear through the tunica intima which permits blood to dissect through the layers of the vessel (eg, media, adventitia). Dissection can involve the ascending and descending aorta, as well as the aortic branches. Classic presentation includes sudden onset tearing chest pain that radiates to the back and increased blood pressure. Other presenting features depend on which aortic branches are involved (eg, neurological deficits with carotid artery involvement, acute kidney injury with renal artery involvement). Diagnosis is confirmed with CT angiography, which will reveal the dissection as well as any other complications, such as branch vessel involvement or rupture with hemorrhage. This patient’s CT scan shows dissection of the descending aorta extending into the celiac trunk (the vessel indicated by the arrow). The celiac trunk is the first major branch of the descending aorta and gives rise to the common hepatic artery, left gastric artery, and splenic artery at T12. It supplies blood to the liver, stomach, proximal duodenum, pancreas, inferior esophagus, and spleen. Primary initial management for all types of aortic dissection involves rapid reduction in blood pressure and pulse to prevent further propagation of the dissection. Intravenous beta blockers are the preferred first-line agent for medical management. Dissection involving the ascending aorta often requires operative repair.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Colon (Choice A) receives its blood supply from both the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) and inferior mesenteric artery (IMA). The cecum, ascending colon, and proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon are supplied by the SMA. The distal third of the transverse colon as well as the upper portion of the rectum are supplied by the IMA.

Kidney (Choice B) receives its blood supply from the renal artery which branches directly from the descending aorta. While a descending aortic dissection may compromise renal blood flow, it would be through involvement of the renal arteries, not the celiac trunk.

Pancreas (Choice C) and small bowel (Choice D) both receive blood supply from two major sources: the celiac trunk and the SMA. The splenic artery is a major division of the celiac trunk whose branches supply a portion of the pancreas. The common hepatic artery, another major branch of the celiac trunk, gives rise to the gastroduodenal artery which then branches into the anterior and posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries that supply part of the pancreas as well as the proximal duodenum. The SMA gives rise to the anterior and posterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries which supply the distal duodenum and part of the pancreatic head. The superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries form an anastomosis. Because of this dual blood supply, the pancreas and small bowel would still receive blood flow through the SMA if dissection occurred through the celiac trunk.

Educational Objective: Aortic dissection classically presents with tearing chest pain and increased blood pressure. Dissection can occur through the ascending or descending aorta, as well as through any of the aortic branches. The celiac trunk is the first major branch of the descending aorta and supplies blood to the liver, stomach, proximal duodenum, pancreas, inferior esophagus, and spleen. Dissection involving the ascending aorta often requires operative repair.

questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of intermittent chest pain that is "not severe but rather annoying." Her mother died of sudden cardiac arrest at age 51 years. A midsystolic click is heard in the fifth intercostal space in the left midclavicular line. Which of the following cardiac abnormalities is most likely in this patient?

options.label: B
options.html: B.    Bicuspid aortic valve with stenosis

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C.

Mitral valve prolapse is a structural cardiac disease characterized by abnormal positioning and movement of the mitral valve leaflets into the left atrium during ventricular contraction. It is more common in females. The most common causes are myxomatous degeneration, chorda tendinae rupture, and mitral annular disjunction, in which the mitral annulus becomes partially detached. Myxomatous degeneration results in thickened mitral valve leaflets due to accumulation of fibrous and mucoid material.

It may be idiopathic or caused by hereditary disease and may be present in muscular dystrophies. It is also associated with connective tissue disorders such as Marfan and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, as well as adult polycystic kidney disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, and polyarteritis nodosa. Patients are typically asymptomatic, but may develop palpitations, chest pain, and dyspnea especially if there is mitral regurgitation. Patients classically have a midsystolic click on cardiac auscultation, which may or may not be followed by the late systolic murmur of mitral regurgitation.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

Atrial septal defect (Choice A) results in a left-to-right shunt with abnormal flow of blood from the left atrium to the right atrium, resulting in relative volume overload of the right atrium and ventricle, which presents as a fixed, split S2, and low-grade physiologic ejection murmur on cardiac auscultation.

Bicuspid aortic valve with stenosis (Choice B) presents with a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur, best heard at the upper right sternal border, and radiates to the carotid arteries. Patients with a congenital bicuspid aortic valve typically present early in adulthood; however, a midsystolic click is more consistent with mitral valve prolapse.

Patent foramen ovale (Choice D) is a common atrial septal defect resulting from failure of the fetal right-to-left shunt to close completely. A patent foramen ovale that persists into adulthood is a risk factor for arterial thromboembolic disease. Cardiac auscultation may reveal a subtle diastolic murmur.

Tricuspid regurgitation (Choice E) classically shows a holosystolic murmur best heard in the left lower sternal border and may result from severe pulmonary hypertension or infective endocarditis in the setting of intravenous drug use.

Educational Objective: Mitral valve prolapse is a structural disease of the mitral valve leaflets resulting in abnormal displacement, movement, and thickening of the leaflets. It is classically associated with a midsystolic click and the presence of mitral regurgitation.

questions.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman comes to the physician because she has not had a menstrual period for 3 months. She also has had increased facial and chest hair growth over the past 2 months. She is 170 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 64 kg (141 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m2. Her pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 140/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows hirsutism and vaginal atrophy. Her serum testosterone concentration is 400 ng/dL (N=15–60), and measurement of urine collection of 17-ketosteroids is 10 mg/24 h. Ultrasonography of the pelvis shows a normal-sized left ovary and a right ovarian mass. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

This patient is presenting with clinical signs and symptoms of virilization, the condition in which females develop male features due to increased concentrations of androgens. These features include hirsutism, or the presence of unwanted hair in a male distribution, increased muscle mass, pubic hair, clitoromegaly, and vaginal atrophy, and are confirmed by her increased testosterone concentration. Testosterone may be increased in the setting of a hormone-secreting ovarian tumor, polycystic ovary syndrome, hypersecretion of androgens by the adrenal gland, or an adrenal tumor. When evaluating virilization and hirsutism, it is critical to measure the concentrations of testosterone and 17-ketosteroids; the latter is made by the adrenal gland and helps to narrow the differential diagnosis. In this case, because testosterone is increased while the 17-ketosteroids are within normal limits, the cause likely has an ovarian source. This is further supported by the presence of a right ovarian mass on ultrasonography. A Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor is a rare, androgen-producing, ovarian sex-cord stromal tumor. It is a neoplastic proliferation of the cells that give rise to the specialized gonadal stroma surrounding the granulosa and theca cells in females and Sertoli and Leydig cells in males.

These proliferating cells have the capacity for differentiation into many cell types, including Sertoli-Leydig cells, which secrete testosterone.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Germ cell tumors (Choice A) are rare and may be benign or malignant tumors that consist of germ cells, most commonly in the ovaries or testes. They present more commonly in females aged 10 to 30 years and include mature teratomas, dysgerminomas, embryonal carcinomas, and other tumors. While these tumors can be hormonally active, they more commonly secrete human chorionic gonadotropin, which would not cause the virilization seen in this patient.

Granulosa tumor (Choice B) is a malignant sex-cord stromal tumor. It produces female sex hormones, which often result in abnormal uterine bleeding. The virilization that this patient is experiencing is more likely secondary to testosterone release from a Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor.

Polycystic ovarian disease (Choice C) presents with menstrual irregularities, signs of androgen excess, obesity, insulin resistance, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasonography. While this patient does have signs of androgen excess with an increased testosterone concentration, she does not exhibit obesity or evidence of polycystic ovaries. Rather, she has a right ovarian mass, making an androgen-secreting Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor more likely.

Thecoma (Choice E) is a rare, most commonly benign, tumor of the ovary. When present, it commonly has estrogenic effects, which may lead to irregular menstrual bleeding. It would not explain this patient’s increased testosterone concentrations and virilization.

Educational Objective: A Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor is a rare, androgen-producing, ovarian sex-cord stromal tumor that may cause precocious puberty or virilization. Hirsutism, or the presence of unwanted hair in a male distribution, increased muscle mass, pubic hair, clitoromegaly, and vaginal atrophy are features of virilization.

questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of increasing hoarseness. He has smoked 2 packs of cigarettes daily for 40 years. Laryngoscopic examination shows a mass consistent with a malignant neoplasm in the larynx, involving the right vestibular fold. This neoplasm is most likely to metastasize initially to which of the following groups of lymph nodes?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A.

Laryngeal neoplasms can present with hoarseness, vocal changes, persistent cough, stridor, or dysphagia. Primary risk factors include human papillomavirus infection and tobacco use. The majority of laryngeal neoplasms are squamous cell carcinoma.

Lesions located in the supraglottic region are likely to induce dysphagia, whereas hoarseness is an early symptom of lesions located in the glottic region due to involvement of the vocal cords.

The diagnosis is established by direct tumor visualization, which may be accomplished with laryngoscopy. The cervical lymph nodes are a common location for metastases from head and neck cancers such as laryngeal carcinoma. CT or PET scan may be useful for characterizing metastatic disease. Early-stage laryngeal carcinoma has a good prognosis, but locally advanced or metastatic disease can be more difficult to treat. Treatment involves surgical excision, including neck dissection, radiotherapy, and/or chemotherapy.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E.

Mediastinal (Choice B) lymph node metastasis is typically associated with malignancies of the trunk, such as lung cancer and melanoma. Mediastinal lymph node involvement is particularly important in determining the prognosis of non-small cell lung cancer.

Submandibular (Choice C) and submental (Choice D) lymph nodes comprise Level I of the anatomic lymph node levels of the neck. While spread of head and neck cancers to these lymph nodes is not as common as it is to cervical lymph nodes, these nodes are commonly among those excised during a modified radical neck dissection for the treatment of locally advanced head and neck cancer.

Supraclavicular (Choice E) lymph node involvement is classically seen in metastatic gastric cancer, though it can also occur in the spread of other sub-diaphragmatic malignancies, such as renal, gonadal, and gastrointestinal cancers. The supraclavicular nodes on the left are known as Virchow nodes.

Educational Objective: Laryngeal neoplasms can present with hoarseness, vocal changes, persistent cough, stridor, or dysphagia. Primary risk factors include human papillomavirus infection and tobacco use. The cervical lymph nodes are a common location for metastasis from laryngeal cancer and other head and neck neoplasms.

questions.stemHtml: A 49-year-old woman with poorly controlled hypertension comes to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of progressive shortness of breath. Current medications are amlodipine, clonidine, enalapril, hydrochlorothiazide, and metoprolol. She has not taken any of her medications for 5 days because she ran out and could not afford to refill her prescriptions. Her pulse is 98/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure is 240/120 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 86%. Physical examination shows no significant ankle edema. Bilateral crackles are heard over all lung fields. Cardiac examination shows a loud S4 . A chest x-ray shows pulmonary edema. An ECG is shown. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient’s congestive heart failure?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C.

This patient with poorly-controlled hypertension, progressive dyspnea, and chest x-ray showing pulmonary edema has symptoms of decompensated heart failure. Based on the presence of an S4 heart sound on auscultation, she likely has underlying diastolic dysfunction. In patients with longstanding uncontrolled hypertension, the cardiac myocytes undergo hypertrophy in response to the chronic increase in afterload. This ventricular hypertrophy and increased muscle mass lead to increased stiffness and decreased compliance of the left ventricle, making it more difficult to fill. An S4 gallop is a heart sound that occurs in late diastole during atrial contraction. It is associated with increased atrial pressure and ventricular hypertrophy as the left atrium attempts to overcome a stiff and noncompliant left ventricle.

Patients with decompensated heart failure can present with multiple symptoms. In left heart failure, patients may present with dyspnea and orthopnea, and often have rales on lung auscultation caused by pulmonary edema from increased left-heart pressure. In advanced cases, or during times of exacerbation, patients may present with decreased peripheral perfusion and cardiogenic shock. In right heart failure, patients may present with peripheral edema, jugular venous distension (JVD), and hepatic congestion.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, E, and F.

Atrial fibrillation (Choice A) is seen as irregularly irregular RR intervals without discernible P waves on ECG. When symptomatic, patients may present with palpitations, fatigue, lightheadedness, and dyspnea. An S4 heart sound and pulmonary crackles more likely suggest diastolic dysfunction and pulmonary edema as a cause of the symptoms.

Cardiac tamponade (Choice B) classically presents with hypotension, jugular venous distension, and muffled heart sounds (Beck triad). ECG may show electrical alternans and low voltage of the QRS complexes. Cardiac tamponade results from rapid and/or excessive accumulation of fluid within the pericardial space impairing right ventricular diastolic filling. Because the diastolic dysfunction in tamponade is right-sided, not left-sided, lung sounds are clear in these patients.

Dilated cardiomyopathy (Choice D) and myocardial ischemia (Choice E) both cause systolic dysfunction in addition to any potential diastolic dysfunction. Clinical presentation can be like that of a patient with diastolic dysfunction with dyspnea, pulmonary edema, peripheral edema, and JVD. However, in cases of systolic dysfunction, an S3 (not an S4) heart sound may be present due to increased ventricular filling pressures, which is usually seen in the setting of volume overload.

Papillary muscle rupture (Choice F) can occur as a complication of myocardial infarction and results in acute mitral regurgitation. This classically occurs 2 to 7 days following a myocardial infarction and presents with acute onset of dyspnea and pulmonary edema due to increased backflow of blood, and potential cardiogenic shock due to decrease of forward flow. A holosystolic murmur can be heard on auscultation.

Educational Objective: Longstanding uncontrolled hypertension can lead to diastolic dysfunction. This occurs secondary to ventricular hypertrophy leading to decreased compliance and reduced ventricular filling. An S4 heart sound may be heard on auscultation. Patients can present with dyspnea, orthopnea, fatigue, and peripheral edema if right heart dysfunction and/or hypervolemia are also present.

questions.stemHtml: A 6-year-old boy is admitted to the hospital because of an 8-hour history of fever, headache, and nausea. Administration of intravenous (IV) fluids and empiric antibiotics is started pending culture results. A lumbar puncture is done, and a photomicrograph of a Gram stain of cerebrospinal fluid is shown. During the next 24 hours, he develops bleeding from his gums and from all IV puncture sites. He is intubated for respiratory failure, and norepinephrine is administered for blood pressure support. The most likely cause of this patient’s new symptoms is which of the following infection-related complications?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A.

This patient’s signs and symptoms of fever, headache, and nausea with gram-negative diplococci in his cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) are consistent with meningococcal disease caused by Neisseria meningitidis. N. meningitidis is a gram-negative diplococcus that can lead to meningitis and may rapidly progress to septic shock.

The organism is transmissible by respiratory droplets. Findings of meningococcal meningitis include fever, altered mental status, headache, and meningeal signs such as neck stiffness and presence of a Brudzinski or Kernig sign. Meningococcemia frequently causes disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), a systemic disorder characterized by the widespread activation of the clotting cascade and resulting in microthrombi formation, thrombocytopenia, and bleeding complications due to consumption of platelets and clotting factors. DIC presents with a characteristic petechial rash, as well as bleeding from mucous membranes and venipuncture sites.

Additionally, severe cases of meningococcal disease may lead to bilateral adrenal gland hemorrhage, a condition known as Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome. Adrenal insufficiency develops rapidly and presents with hypotension, hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, and hypoglycemia due to deficiency of aldosterone and glucocorticoids. The diagnosis of meningococcal disease is confirmed by culture of blood or CSF. Treatment includes supportive therapy and broad-spectrum antibiotics, typically with a third-generation cephalosporin. DIC is treated with transfusion of fresh frozen plasma or cryoprecipitate, while adrenal insufficiency requires supplementation of glucocorticoids in addition to vasopressor support. Meningococcal disease causes substantial morbidity and mortality even with appropriate therapy, although infection may be prevented with meningococcal vaccine.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E.

Cerebral edema (Choice B) may occur in the setting of bacterial meningitis or secondary to other inflammatory, hemodynamic, or ischemic insults. While cerebral edema may lead to headache, obtundation, nausea, vomiting, and cranial nerve or neurologic deficits, it does not typically cause hypotension. In fact, cerebral edema and accompanying increased intracranial pressure are more likely to present with hypertension, as well as bradycardia and irregular breathing, known as the Cushing triad.

Congestive heart failure (Choice C) is incorrect. While patients with meningococcemia may present with hypotension, this is caused by septic shock rather than cardiogenic shock.

Pulmonary embolism (Choice D) is incorrect. While DIC is defined by widespread activation of the clotting cascade, this tends to present with microthrombi and diffuse bleeding rather than macroscopic thrombosis.

Toxic epidermal necrolysis (Choice E) is a life-threatening adverse cutaneous reaction, often a drug reaction. Features such as skin pain, sloughing, or mucosal involvement are suggestive of toxic epidermal necrolysis. Frequently implicated drugs include sulfa and beta-lactam antibiotics as well as anticonvulsants, including carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin, and valproic acid.

Educational Objective: Meningococcal disease is caused by the gram-negative diplococcus Neisseria meningitidis and may present with severe clinical manifestations, including meningitis, sepsis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and bilateral adrenal hemorrhage, also known as Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome. Adrenal insufficiency presents with hypotension, hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, and hypoglycemia due to deficiency of aldosterone and glucocorticoids. Meningococcal disease causes substantial morbidity and mortality even with appropriate therapy, although infection may be prevented with meningococcal vaccine.

questions.stemHtml: A 43-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of intermittent abdominal pain. The pain occurs after fatty meals and is localized to the right upper quadrant. Ultrasonography of the abdomen shows cholelithiasis. The patient elects to begin a trial of ursodiol therapy before considering operative treatment. Which of the following is the primary mechanism of action of this medication?

options.label: A
options.html: A.     Decreased cholesterol secretion into bile

options.label: D
options.html: D.     Inhibition of bile acid synthesis

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A.

The classic presentation of cholelithiasis is intermittent right upper quadrant pain and nausea that is worse with eating in a middle-aged female. Cholesterol gallstones are the most common type of gallstones, and risk factors for their development include obesity, advanced age, estrogen therapy, rapid weight loss, and Crohn disease. Inhibition of biliary cholesterol secretion is achieved by the use of ursodeoxycholic acid (ursodiol), a medication used to treat biliary colic, primary biliary cirrhosis, and intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. In patients who have atypical symptoms that are not definitively attributable to gallstones, improvement with ursodiol suggests that cholecystectomy may be beneficial, but in patients with classic biliary colic, as in this patient, ursodiol is considered a second line to surgery. It works by reducing cholesterol secretion from the liver by 40% to 60%, and thereby reducing the cholesterol content of the bile. It also reduces the amount of cholesterol absorbed in the gut. As most gallstones are made of cholesterol, with a minority formed from heme because of chronic hemolysis, gradually reducing the amount of cholesterol in the bile prevents formation of new cholesterol gallstones.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E.

Enhanced cholesterol absorption (Choice B) and enhanced hepatic cholesterol synthesis (Choice C) would both increase the risk for formation of cholesterol gallstones by increasing serum cholesterol levels. This could lead to worsening of this patient’s condition.

Inhibition of bile acid synthesis (Choice D) would increase the risk for formation of cholesterol gallstones. The fibrates are a class of medications that inhibit the rate limiting enzyme in bile acid synthesis, cholesterol 7-α-hydroxylase. Reduction of bile acid synthesis leads to bile that is supersaturated with cholesterol, making it more likely for stones to precipitate.

Inhibition of 3-HMG-CoA (Choice E) is the mechanism of statin drugs. HMG-CoA reductase catalyzes the rate limiting step in cholesterol biosynthesis, thereby resulting in reduced intrahepatic levels of cholesterol. There is evidence that patients taking a statin may be at lower risk for developing gallstones, but statins are not currently used for this purpose.

Educational Objective: Ursodiol decreases the cholesterol content of bile and thereby prevents the formation of cholesterol gallstones. It is considered second-line therapy when compared to cholecystectomy in patients with cholelithiasis who present with classic biliary colic.
