questions.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of intense pain on the right side of her body. She describes the pain as a constant, burning sensation of variable intensity. Over-the-counter medications have not resolved her pain. Six months ago, she sustained a cerebral infarction accompanied by loss of sensation over the right side. Neurologic examination shows loss of sensation to light touch and proprioception on the right side. Light touch of the skin elicits pain. No motor deficits were detected. The most likely cause of this patient’s condition is a lesion in which of the following labeled areas in the MRI of a normal brain?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C.

Choice C identifies the thalamus, a gray matter region with diverse roles including relaying sensory and motor information and mediating alertness. The spinothalamic tract, which mediates the sensation of pain, feeds into the thalamus. Cerebrovascular accidents (CVAs, also known as strokes) occur because of ischemic or hemorrhagic loss of blood supply to the brain. Classically, CVAs manifest as a neurologic deficit related to the affected part of the brain. If the thalamus is infarcted, patients may lose the ability to accurately interpret sensory information, and if the spinothalamic tract is affected, may also experience a centralized poststroke pain syndrome called thalamic pain syndrome. Thalamic pain syndrome may occur in the acute poststroke phase or months or years after a stroke. It is characterized by an initial loss of sensation or paresthesia followed by burning pain with allodynia. These sensory symptoms typically involve the entire contralateral half of the patient’s body, but in some cases, are poorly localized. Treatment may involve both pharmacological strategies (eg, tricyclic antidepressants, anticonvulsants) and nonpharmacologic strategies (eg, physical therapy, cognitive-behavioral therapy).

Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

Choice A identifies the caudate nucleus. The caudate nucleus is a basal ganglia structure located directly lateral to the lateral ventricles that modulates motor control along with higher order functions, such as learning, memory, motivation, and emotion. Lesions of the caudate nucleus lead to disinhibition and agitation.

Choice B identifies the internal capsule. The internal capsule primarily contains the descending corticospinal tract, though it also contains axons of various additional pathways, including third-order sensory neurons traveling from the thalamus to the primary sensory cortex. Internal capsule lacunar infarcts may present with purely motor deficits that cause contralateral hemiparesis, ataxic hemiparesis (ie, contralateral hemiparesis plus ataxia), clumsy hand-dysarthria (ie, hand weakness plus articulation difficulties), or occasionally, motor weakness plus sensory symptoms. The combination of loss of sensation and centralized pain is uncommon in internal capsule strokes.

Choice D identifies the Broca convolution. In a CVA, lesions involving this area can result in expressive (Broca) aphasia.

Choice E identifies the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe. The role of this brain area is to process visual information, not light touch, proprioception, or pain.

Educational Objective: Thalamic pain syndrome is a centralized poststroke pain syndrome caused by a thalamic infarction characterized by loss of sensation, burning pain, and allodynia. These sensory symptoms typically involve the entire contralateral half of the patient’s body, but in some cases, are poorly localized.

The caudate nucleus is a basal ganglia structure located directly lateral to the lateral ventricles that modulates motor control along with higher order functions, such as learning, memory, motivation, and emotion. Lesions of the caudate nucleus lead to disinhibition and agitation.

Choice B identifies the internal capsule. The internal capsule primarily contains the descending corticospinal tract, though it also contains axons of various additional pathways, including third-order sensory neurons traveling from the thalamus to the primary sensory cortex. Internal capsule lacunar infarcts may present with purely motor deficits that cause contralateral hemiparesis, ataxic hemiparesis (ie, contralateral hemiparesis plus ataxia), clumsy hand-dysarthria (ie, hand weakness plus articulation difficulties), or occasionally, motor weakness plus sensory symptoms. The combination of loss of sensation and centralized pain is uncommon in internal capsule strokes.

Choice D identifies the Broca convolution. In a CVA, lesions involving this area can result in expressive (Broca) aphasia.

Choice E identifies the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe. The role of this brain area is to process visual information, not light touch, proprioception, or pain.

Educational Objective: Thalamic pain syndrome is a centralized poststroke pain syndrome caused by a thalamic infarction characterized by loss of sensation, burning pain, and allodynia. These sensory symptoms typically involve the entire contralateral half of the patient’s body, but in some cases, are poorly localized.

questions.stemHtml: A homeless 30-year-old man who is living in a shelter is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of cough productive of bloody sputum. A chest x-ray shows a cavitary lesion in the right upper lobe and calcifications in the right hilum. An acid-fast smear of sputum is positive. Sputum is inoculated into mycobacterial culture media. Which of the following best represents the expected time before positive culture results will be available?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a slow-growing organism transmitted via respiratory secretions. It causes tuberculosis, which presents with systemic symptoms including fever, night sweats, and weight loss, as well as pulmonary symptoms such as cough and hemoptysis. The slow growth and evasion of immune defenses result in the disease presenting with primary, latent, and reactivation patterns. While uncommon in the developed world, tuberculosis remains prevalent among patients who are homeless, incarcerated, or immunocompromised. The diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis requires isolation of M. tuberculosis from sputum cultures. However, given the slow-growing nature of M. tuberculosis, sputum cultures do not yield results for several weeks. Other diagnostic tests, such as interferon gamma release assays and chest x-rays, may provide useful clinical information while culture results are pending. The chest x-ray in reactivation tuberculosis classically shows cavitary lesions in the apices of the lung, with possible evidence of a Ghon complex (pulmonary calcified granulomas and hilar adenopathy) from a prior primary tuberculous infection. It is typically necessary to begin empiric antibiotic treatment prior to confirmatory culture results in patients suspected of having tuberculosis. Active disease is treated primarily with a combination of rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Less than 24 hours (Choice A) is the appropriate time frame for results of an interferon gamma release assay.

2–3 days (Choice B) is the appropriate time frame for the interpretation of a tuberculin skin test. Tuberculin skin testing is appropriate for screening for prior exposure to tuberculosis in asymptomatic patients.

4–7 days (Choice C) is incorrect. While many bacterial and fungal cultures produce results within days, M. tuberculosis is not generally detectable on culture media for several weeks.

4–6 months (Choice E) is incorrect. While M. tuberculosis is slow-growing, most culture protocols can detect the organism at a maximum of 6–8 weeks.

questions.stemHtml: A 41-year-old man has the acute onset of abdominal pain caused by a calculus at the right ureterovesical junction. The pain is most likely to radiate to which of the following locations on the right?

options.label: B
options.html: B.       Upper quadrant of the abdomen

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C.

Nephrolithiasis or ureterolithiasis describes the formation of calculi within the urinary collecting system, otherwise known as kidney or ureteral stones. Calcium oxalate stones are the most common type (making up generally 80% of all urinary tract calculi), though calcium phosphate, struvite, uric acid, and proteinaceous stones (eg, cystine) are also seen. Diagnosis is through non-contrast CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis. Treatment varies depending on the size, location, and complicating features. Small, uncomplicated stones often pass without intervention, whereas large, obstructing, or infected stones may require antibiotics, surgical removal, ureteral stenting, or percutaneous nephrostomy. There are three common sites where ureteral stones lodge caused by narrowing in the ureter: the ureteropelvic junction, where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels, and the ureterovesical junction. Sensory fibers that innervate the ureters enter the spinal cord at T12 through L2, and pain from the ureter is referred to those dermatomes around the groin.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

Pain at the costovertebral angle (Choice A) would be more suggestive of pyelonephritis, with inflammation and infection of the kidney itself. Pyelonephritis commonly presents with fever, flank pain, and costovertebral angle tenderness. Pain in this location could occur from nephrolithiasis if the stone were obstructing with resultant hydronephrosis.

Pain that radiates to the upper quadrant of the abdomen (Choice B) typically is caused by cholecystitis, cholelithiasis, pancreatitis, or gastritis.

Pain that radiates to the lower leg or foot (Choices D and E) is often caused by pathologies that affect the L4, L5, and S1 dermatomes, such as sciatica.

Educational Objective: Sensory nerves from T12 to L2 innervate the ureters. Pain associated with ureterolithiasis is commonly referred to those dermatomal areas around the groin.
